summary:
SPHEREx Blink is a public web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx images into a short movie of any patch of sky, so that anything that moves or changes brightness stands out.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared colours, but the data arrive as millions of 65 MB files in which every exposure records a different colour. Nobody can simply flip through them. With SPHEREx Blink, a user types a sky position or object name. The tool finds every SPHEREx exposure of that patch, cleans and aligns them, and plays one frame per sky pass. A Subtract view removes everything that stayed the same, so a moving object appears as a bright spot beside a dark one. 

Clicking any object gives its infrared spectrum and light curve, built on the fly.
Most known brown dwarfs and many comets were found by volunteers blinking images. SPHEREx Blink brings that method to NASA's newest sky survey, with nothing to install, so more people can help find the Sun's undiscovered neighbours.
details:
What it does

• Search by Right Ascension and declination, or by object name. Fast-moving objects are centred on where they are now.

• Blink: one cleaned, aligned picture per sky pass (or per month, week or day), with play, step and scrub controls.

• Subtract and Add: subtract other epochs to reveal movers, or stack all epochs for depth.

• 102 colours: choose one of the six detector bands, drag any wavelength range on a ruler, make three-band colour pictures, or map water ice, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, hydrogen lines and cold objects in one click.

• Spectra on the fly: click any object for its spectrum and its brightness over time.

• Overlays: Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 markers that move with each star's known motion to the date of each frame, plus an Aladin Lite panel for other surveys.

• Metadata: every exposure behind the frame on screen, with its quality flags explained and a link to the original file.

• Field of view from 3 to 20 arcminutes, and the whole view is stored in the URL so it can be shared or embedded in other sites.

How it works

1. A Python server asks the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive which SPHEREx exposures cover the position.

2. Instead of downloading 65 MB per exposure, it reads only the few hundred kilobytes around the target from the SPHEREx mirror on AWS. We checked this against the archive's own cutout service and the pixels were identical.

3. Detector defects and cosmic-ray hits are masked using SPHEREx's flag data, and the zodiacal-light background is removed.

4. Each exposure is aligned onto a common north-up grid and averaged per epoch and detector (the movie frames) and per epoch and spectral channel (a 102-channel cube).

5. Brightness is measured on every single exposure. Because each exposure sees a different wavelength, the measurements form a spectrum.

6. The browser does all scaling, subtraction and charting itself, so controls respond instantly.

Results on the challenge's test targets

• Barnard's Star: a clear northward shift between passes, with the Gaia marker tracking it. The star saturates SPHEREx, so its spectrum is shown as a lower limit.

• Epsilon Indi B: a clear moving pair (4.7 arcseconds per year) and a spectrum showing the methane and water bands of a brown dwarf.

• WISE 0855: a 4 to 5 micron excess at the predicted position, consistent with this very cold brown dwarf, though blended with a background star at shorter wavelengths.

• RW Aurigae and R Draconis: both are bright enough to saturate SPHEREx. The tool flags this instead of plotting wrong numbers.

Benefits and intended impact

It opens the newest NASA sky survey to volunteers, students and researchers through a web address. It could be embedded in a citizen-science project in the spirit of Backyard Worlds, used in classrooms to watch a star move, or used by astronomers for a quick look at any position.

How it is creative

• It turns SPHEREx's awkward design, where every exposure is a different colour, into a feature: the same downloads give a movie, a spectrum and a light curve.

• Catalogue markers move through time, so what is already known is marked and an unmarked mover is a candidate discovery.

• One-click maps that subtract neighbouring wavelengths make ice, molecules or cold objects light up.

• Reading under 2% of each file makes on-demand queries of any position practical on a free server.

Tools and technologies

Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy and Astropy on the server; plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript in the browser; Aladin Lite; pytest; Docker; GitHub Pages.
dataRefs: SPHEREx Level 2 Spectral Images, Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3 (NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive): the images and quality flags shown in the tool.
SPHEREx on AWS Open Data (bucket nasa-irsa-spherex): where the pixels are read from.
IRSA Simple Image Access (SIA2) and TAP services: used to find which exposures cover a position.
SPHEREx spectral calibration products (spectral channel table and per-pixel wavelength tables): give the wavelength of every pixel and define the 102 channels.
IRSA cutout service: used to validate our own cutouts.
SPHEREx archive documentation and IRSA tutorial notebooks: file layout, flag definitions and access methods.
CatWISE2020 catalogue (from NASA's WISE and NEOWISE missions): infrared source overlay with proper motions
WiseView (NASA-funded Backyard Worlds project): design inspiration.
